newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel head says rate cuts hinge on budget.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel head says rate cuts hinge on budget.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said in an interview published on Thursday that significant interest rate cuts would not come until he saw that budget cuts were being successfully implemented.

"The fact that (the budget cuts) were approved is very important, but you must remeber that in past years the government had good budget plans, only the implementation was faulty. Therefore the real test this year will be in implementation," Frenkel said in an interview published in the daily newspaper Haaretz.

The 1997 budget calls for spending cuts, new taxes and other revenue-raising measures totalling about seven billion shekels, which are aimed at keeping the deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.
"If it becomes clear that there is no (monetary) injection from the government due to overspending this year it will make possible a more balanced mix in monetary policy," Frenkel said.
Frenkel said he did not see either the budget or the slowdown in inflation in the second half of 1996 as reasons yet to ease off the bank's tight monetary regime.
"It would be a mistake to declare victory and withdraw," he said. "The struggle with inflation continues."
Frenkel said monetary policy had contributed to the reduction in inflation in the second half of 1996.

"I have no doubt that the restrictive monetary policy that began in the second quarter made an important contribution to putting brakes on inflation, to lowering inflationary expectations and after several months to an actual reduction of inflation," he said.

Consumer prices were running at a 14.6 percent annual rate in first-half 1996, slowing to half that rate in the second. The Bank of Israel's base rate peaked in mid-year at 17 percent but has since fallen to 14.7 percent.
For the full year, inflation was 10.6 percent, slightly above the government's target for the year of eight to 10 percent.
